units.title: Test a call-back widget that connects web leads to sales

claim.text: The source describes a call-back widget where a visitor enters a phone number and clicks call me now; the system calls the business first, whispers who called from the website, then calls the lead back from a number that looks like the business's, connecting the sales team. The source also observed increased other conversions, including direct phone numbers, says it can record calls like Response Tap, and gives pricing of $49/month on the annual plan or $59, including some phone numbers/calls.
claim.quote: So, they just put in their phone number and click call me now. And then it what it does is it calls you first, whispers to tell you that this is, you know, someone so and so has called from the website and then it calls them back. So, the person gets a phone call from a phone number that looks like yours and it connects your sales team with that person. Obviously, this only works if you've got people on the phones that are, you know, ready to go right now and you've got a sales team that you're happy they're kind of half inbound, half outbound calls really. Um, but it's fantastic. It's fantastic for two reasons. Not only do you get calls through this, but we've also noticed it um increase other conversions, including direct phone numbers. So, just by having the call widget and offering to call people back, we've noticed that it increases the number of people that actually call you directly, as crazy as that sounds. So, it's a really good tool. It's very cheap. I don't know exactly how much it is, but it doesn't cost much. Let's just have a look here. So yeah, $49 a month if you're on the annual plan or 59 um and that includes some of the phone number uh some of the phone calls as well.

action.quote: So this is something that I would test definitely.

args.text: People are on the phones and ready to take calls now.
args.quote: you've got people on the phones that are, you know, ready to go right now

args.text: The business has a sales team comfortable with half inbound, half outbound calls.
args.quote: you've got a sales team that you're happy they're kind of half inbound, half outbound calls really.

units.title: Use tawk.to for live chat

claim.text: The source recommends tawk.to as a free live chat tool that does everything expected; its business model sells agents to man the chat, but the software is free to use whether or not the business pays for agents. The source also notes admin area, team accounts, roundrobin availability, schedule opening/closing hours, offline message taking, and a mobile app.
claim.quote: This is talk to so t awk t awk. And it's free which is mental um because it's really good. It does everything that you would want a live chat software to do. It's a crazy business model they've got. Basically they make money by selling people to man the live chat. So, they give the software away free and they're hoping that you pay for their agents to man the live chat for you. Whether or not you do that, take advantage of the fact that this is an amazing tool and I can't believe that they're giving it away free. They could easily charge because it's as powerful as most of the paid tools. Um, really nice admin area. You can log in. You can give your team different accounts. Um, which means that when people are available, they can be put into the roundrobin to get the chats. You can schedule times as well. So, people are often worried. They think, you know, I don't want to be tied to my phone or tied to my computer at all hours of the day. Um, but you don't have to be because you set your opening and closing hours and then it's, you know, it's it's um it's only online when you are and then the rest of the time they just take a message.

action.text: Use tawk.to for live chat and do not bother with other live chat software.
action.quote: I wouldn't even bother with any other live chat software to be honest.

unknowns: Phrase 'I can't really recommend it anymore' is ambiguous; context suggests a strong recommendation, but a literal reading could be negative.
Mobile app is mentioned but not detailed.

units.title: Add alert bars for sitewide calls to action

claim.text: The source describes alert bars as sticky elements at the top or bottom of a page that can carry a sitewide call to action. It gives an example with options for call, email, and technical call back, plus a reviews widget, and says this builds credibility and ease of use.
claim.quote: So, there's loads of different providers of alert bars, but an alert bar is basically a sticky thing that sticks at the top of the page or the bottom of the page. The great thing about alert bars is you can put a sitewide call to action on them.

action.text: Consider using alert bars to place sitewide calls to action.
action.quote: something I would definitely recommend looking into

unknowns: No specific alert bar provider is named beyond the implied Leadpages option.

units.title: Use Leadpages for landing pages

claim.text: The source says Leadpages also provides landing pages: standalone pages for paid traffic, usually with a big call to action. They can be added to a site by placing a small piece of code in the header area, after designing the page in Leadpages.
claim.quote: The great thing about lead pages is you've got some landing pages as well that you can build. So, landing pages are just standalone pages uh that you can run paid traffic to usually with a big fat call to action on. Um, it's a really simple way of adding these things to your site without having to get all technical and without having to, you know, build stuff because you just put a little piece of code. You design it all in lead pages and then you put a little piece of code um in the header area on your site and then you've got that.

action.text: Use Leadpages to build standalone landing pages for paid traffic with a strong call to action.
action.quote: landing pages are just standalone pages uh that you can run paid traffic to usually with a big fat call to action on.

unknowns: No specific paid traffic channels or campaign details are provided.

claim.text: The source presents six elements for analyzing live websites: credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease of use, and result, each with a guiding question.
claim.quote: So the six elements that we're going to be going through and I'm just going to bring them onto the screen so you can see them. Um so that is credibility lure. So let's talk through them first. So credibility. So how many credibility triggers do we see on the pages? Um is it clear that this business actually you know has reason to talk about what they're talking about? Uh lure. So how attractive is the thing that they're using to get us to become a lead? Objection handling. Are they removing any potential fears or objections that we might have about requesting that thing? Social proof. Is it obvious that other people have chosen this business? Ease of use. How easy is it to become a lead or sale? Um are there any kind of impediments in the way? And then finally, result. Is it clear that we're going to get a particular result when we take the action that they want us to take?

claim.text: Credibility element: assess how many credibility triggers appear on pages and whether it is clear the business has reason to talk about the topic.
claim.quote: So credibility. So how many credibility triggers do we see on the pages? Um is it clear that this business actually you know has reason to talk about what they're talking about?

claim.text: Objection handling element: assess whether potential fears or objections about requesting the thing are removed.
claim.quote: Objection handling. Are they removing any potential fears or objections that we might have about requesting that thing?

claim.text: Social proof element: assess whether it is obvious that other people have chosen the business.
claim.quote: Social proof. Is it obvious that other people have chosen this business?

claim.text: Ease of use element: assess how easy it is to become a lead or sale and whether any impediments exist.
claim.quote: Ease of use. How easy is it to become a lead or sale? Um are there any kind of impediments in the way?

claim.text: Result element: assess whether it is clear that the visitor will get a particular result when taking the desired action.
claim.quote: And then finally, result. Is it clear that we're going to get a particular result when we take the action that they want us to take?

units.title: Owen Mitchell homepage lacks clear solicitor positioning

claim.text: Example: Owen Mitchell homepage uses 'expert hand, human touch', which does not make clear that the firm is a solicitor's firm; the source would prefer using targeted phrases like 'UK's leading solicitors firm' to set the scene.
claim.quote: So the homepage, first of all, expert hand, human touch. The problem that we have with this, even the first two lines here, is it's not clear that they're actually a solicitor's firm. Okay, expert hand, human touch. What does that actually mean? It means almost nothing. Um, so it's from a marketing perspective, I get what they're trying to do. They're trying to be the friendly and approachable side. I would much rather from a digital marketing perspective that they actually use some of the phrases that they're targeting like national, you know, UK's leading uh solicitors firm or something like that where they set the scene and tell people without any shadow of a doubt this is what we do.

units.title: Homepage sets scene; subpages accept cold traffic

claim.text: For subpage-driven businesses, the homepage should still set the scene, and subpages should be ready to accept cold traffic.
claim.quote: whilst not many people will be coming through the homepage, we still need to do a good job on the homepage of setting the scene and then we need to make sure that subpages are ready to accept cold traffic as well.

units.title: Alert bar conversion may be lower than an embedded form

claim.text: Warning: alert bars may convert less well than a form built into the page, but should still convert better than no alert bar, so testing is worthwhile.
claim.quote: Now, you might not get as good a conversion rate with an alert bar as you do with a form actually built into the page, but you're going to get a better conversion rate than without it. So, it's certainly worth testing.
